title: “I Am Colin”
paragraphs: When Mary went down to her supper, she carried the picture back to the house and showed it to Martha.
“Eh!” said Martha, bursting with pride. “I never knew our Dickon was so clever. That’s a picture of a missel thrush on her nest, big as life an’ twice as natural.”

Then Mary understood that Dickon had meant the picture as a message. He was telling her she could trust him to keep her secret. Her garden was her nest, and she was like the missel thrush. Oh, how she liked that odd, plain-spoken boy!
She hoped he would come back the very next day. She fell asleep looking forward to the morning.

But you can never tell what the weather will do in Yorkshire, especially in springtime. In the night Mary was woken by heavy raindrops beating against her window. The rain was coming down in torrents, and the wind was “wuthering” around the corners and through the chimneys of the huge old house. Mary sat up in bed, feeling miserable and angry.
“The rain is as contrary as I ever was,” she said. “It came because it knew I didn’t want it.”

She threw herself back on her pillow and buried her face in it. She did not cry, but she lay there hating the sound of the pounding rain, and she hated the wind and its “wuthering.” She could not get back to sleep. The mournful sound kept her awake because she felt mournful herself. If she had been happy, it would probably have lulled her to sleep. How it “wuthered,” and how the big raindrops poured down and beat against the windowpane!
“It sounds just like someone lost on the moor, wandering on and on and crying,” she said.
She had been lying awake for about an hour, tossing from side to side, when suddenly something made her sit up in bed and turn her head toward the door. She listened and listened.
“That isn’t the wind now,” she said in a loud whisper. “It’s different. It’s that crying I heard before.”

Her bedroom door was open a crack, and the sound came down the corridor, a faint, far-off sound of fretful crying. She listened for a few minutes, and with each minute she grew more certain. She felt she had to find out what it was. It seemed even stranger than the secret garden and the buried key. Perhaps being in a rebellious mood made her bold. She put one foot out of bed and stood on the floor.
“I am going to find out what it is,” she said. “Everyone is in bed, and I don’t care about Mrs. Medlock—I don’t care!”

A candle stood by her bedside. She picked it up and went quietly out of the room. The corridor looked very long and dark, but she was too excited to mind. She thought she remembered which corners to turn to reach the short corridor with the tapestry-covered door—the one Mrs. Medlock had come through the day Mary got lost. The sound had come up that passage. So she went on with her dim light, almost feeling her way, her heart beating so loudly that she imagined she could hear it. The faint, far-off crying went on and led her forward. Sometimes it stopped for a moment and then began again. Was this the right corner? She stopped and thought. Yes, it was. Down this passage, then left, then up two broad steps, then right again. Yes, there was the tapestry door.

She pushed it open very gently and closed it behind her. Standing in the corridor, she could hear the crying quite plainly, though it was not loud. It came from the other side of the wall on her left, and a few yards farther on there was a door. A glimmer of light showed beneath it. Someone was crying in that room, and it was quite a young Someone.
So she walked to the door and pushed it open, and there she was, standing in the room!

It was a big room with old, handsome furniture. A low fire glowed faintly on the hearth, and a night light burned beside a carved four-poster bed hung with brocade. On the bed lay a boy, crying fretfully.
Mary wondered whether she was in a real place, or whether she had fallen asleep again and was dreaming without knowing it.

The boy had a sharp, delicate face the color of ivory, and his eyes seemed too big for it. He also had a lot of hair, which tumbled over his forehead in heavy locks and made his thin face look smaller. He looked like a boy who had been ill, but he was crying more like someone tired and cross than like someone in pain.

Mary stood near the door with her candle in her hand, holding her breath. Then she crept across the room. As she came closer, the light caught the boy’s attention. He turned his head on his pillow and stared at her, his gray eyes opening so wide that they looked immense.
“Who are you?” he said at last, in a half-frightened whisper. “Are you a ghost?”
“No, I’m not,” Mary answered, her own whisper sounding half frightened. “Are you?”

He stared and stared and stared. Mary couldn’t help noticing what strange eyes he had. They were agate gray, and they looked too big for his face because they were ringed all around with black lashes.
“No,” he replied, after waiting a moment. “I’m Colin.”
“Who is Colin?” she asked shakily.
“I’m Colin Craven. Who are you?”
“I’m Mary Lennox. Mr. Craven is my uncle.”
“He’s my father,” said the boy.
“Your father!” gasped Mary. “Nobody ever told me he had a son! Why not?”
“Come here,” he said, still keeping his strange eyes fixed on her with an anxious look.
She came close to the bed, and he put out his hand and touched her.
“You’re real, aren’t you?” he said. “I often have dreams that feel very real. You could be one of them.”
Mary had pulled on a woolen wrapper before leaving her room, and now she put a corner of it between his fingers.
“Feel this and you’ll know how thick and warm it is,” she said. “If you like, I’ll pinch you a bit, to prove I’m real. For a moment I wondered if you were a dream as well.”
“Where did you come from?” he asked.
“From my own room. The wind was wuthering so loudly that I couldn’t sleep, and I heard someone crying and wanted to find out who it was. Why were you crying?”
“Because I couldn’t sleep either, and my head ached. Tell me your name again.”
“Mary Lennox. Didn’t anyone ever tell you I’d come to live here?”
He was still fingering the fold of her wrapper, but he was beginning to look a little more as if he believed she was real.
“No,” he answered. “They wouldn’t dare.”
“Why?” asked Mary.
“Because I would have been afraid you’d see me. I won’t let people see me and talk about me.”
“Why?” Mary asked again, feeling more puzzled every moment.

“Because I’m like this all the time, ill and having to lie down. My father won’t let people talk about me either. The servants aren’t allowed to speak of me. If I live, I might turn into a hunchback, but I won’t live. My father hates the thought that I might be like him.”
“Oh, this is such a strange house!” Mary said. “So strange! Everything here is a kind of secret. Rooms are shut away, gardens are shut away—and you! Have they shut you away too?”
“No. I stay in this room because I don’t want to be moved out of it. It tires me too much.”
“Does your father come to see you?” Mary ventured.
“Sometimes. Usually when I’m asleep. He doesn’t want to see me.”
“Why?” Mary couldn’t help asking again.
A kind of angry shadow crossed the boy’s face.
“My mother died the day I was born, and he can’t look at me without feeling wretched. He thinks I don’t know, but I’ve heard people talk. He nearly hates me.”
“He hates the garden because she died,” said Mary, half to herself.
“What garden?” the boy asked.
“Oh! Just—just a garden she used to like,” Mary stammered. “Have you always been here?”

“Almost always. Now and then I’ve been taken to the seaside, but I never stay, because people stare at me. I used to wear an iron brace to hold my back straight. Then a famous doctor came from London to examine me and said the brace was silly. He ordered them to take it off and keep me outdoors in the fresh air. I hate fresh air, and I don’t want to go outside.”
“I didn’t either, when I first came here,” said Mary. “Why do you keep looking at me like that?”
“Because of the dreams that feel so real,” he answered, rather fretfully. “Sometimes when I open my eyes, I don’t believe I’m awake.”

“We’re both awake,” said Mary. She glanced around the room with its high ceiling, shadowy corners and dim firelight. “It looks quite like a dream, and it’s the middle of the night, and everyone in the house is asleep—everyone but us. We’re wide awake.”
“I don’t want it to be a dream,” the boy said restlessly.
Mary suddenly thought of something.
“If you don’t like people to see you,” she began, “do you want me to go away?”
He was still holding the fold of her wrapper, and he gave it a little tug.
“No,” he said. “If you went, I’d be sure you were a dream. If you’re real, sit down on that big footstool and talk. I want to hear about you.”

Mary set her candle on the table near the bed and sat down on the cushioned stool. She didn’t want to go away at all. She wanted to stay in that mysterious, hidden-away room and talk to the mysterious boy.
“What do you want me to tell you?” she said.

He wanted to know how long she had been at Misselthwaite. He wanted to know which corridor her room was on. He wanted to know what she had been doing, whether she disliked the moor the way he did, and where she had lived before she came to Yorkshire. She answered all these questions and many more, and he lay back on his pillow and listened. He made her tell him a great deal about India and about her voyage across the ocean. She found out that, because he had been an invalid, he had not learned things the way other children had. One of his nurses had taught him to read when he was quite little, and he was always reading and looking at the pictures in splendid books.

His father rarely saw him when he was awake, but he was given all sorts of wonderful things to amuse himself with. Still, he never seemed to have been amused. He could have anything he asked for, and he was never made to do anything he didn’t want to do.
“Everyone has to do what pleases me,” he said, without interest. “Getting angry makes me ill. No one believes I’ll live to grow up.”

He said it as if he was so used to the idea that it had stopped mattering to him at all. He seemed to like the sound of Mary’s voice. As she went on talking, he listened in a drowsy, interested way. Once or twice she wondered whether he was slowly drifting off to sleep. But at last he asked a question that opened up a new subject.
“How old are you?” he asked.
“I’m ten,” answered Mary, forgetting herself for a moment, “and so are you.”
“How do you know that?” he demanded, sounding surprised.
“Because the garden door was locked and the key was buried when you were born. And it has been locked for ten years.”
Colin half sat up, turning toward her and leaning on his elbows.
“What garden door was locked? Who did it? Where was the key buried?” he exclaimed, as if he had suddenly become very interested.
“It—it was the garden Mr. Craven hates,” said Mary nervously. “He locked the door. No one—no one knew where he buried the key.”
“What sort of garden is it?” Colin pressed eagerly.
“No one has been allowed to go into it for ten years,” was Mary’s careful answer.

But it was too late to be careful. He was too much like her. He had never had anything to think about either, and a hidden garden pulled at him just as it had pulled at her. He fired off question after question. Where was it? Had she never searched for the door? Had she never asked the gardeners?
“They won’t talk about it,” said Mary. “I think they’ve been told not to answer questions.”
“I’d make them,” said Colin.
“Could you?” Mary faltered, beginning to feel frightened. If he could make people answer questions, who knew what might happen!
“Everyone has to please me. I told you that,” he said. “If I lived, this place would belong to me someday. They all know that. I’d make them tell me.”

Mary had never realized that she herself had been spoiled, but she could plainly see that this mysterious boy was. He believed the whole world was his. How odd he was, and how calmly he talked about not living.
“Do you think you won’t live?” she asked, partly because she was curious and partly in the hope of making him forget the garden.

“I don’t suppose I will,” he answered, as indifferently as before. “For as long as I can remember, I’ve heard people say I won’t. At first they thought I was too little to understand, and now they think I can’t hear. But I can. My doctor is my father’s cousin. He is quite poor, and if I die, he will get all of Misselthwaite when my father is dead. I’d think he wouldn’t want me to live.”
“Do you want to live?” Mary asked.
“No,” he answered, in a cross, tired way. “But I don’t want to die. When I feel ill, I lie here and think about it until I cry and cry.”
“I’ve heard you crying three times,” Mary said, “but I didn’t know who it was. Were you crying about that?” She wanted so badly for him to forget the garden.
“I dare say,” he answered. “Let’s talk about something else. Talk about that garden. Don’t you want to see it?”
“Yes,” answered Mary, in quite a low voice.

“Well, I do,” he went on stubbornly. “I don’t think I ever truly wanted to see anything before, but I want to see that garden. Have the key dug up. Have the door unlocked. They can carry me there in my chair. That would count as fresh air. I’ll make them open the door.”
He had become quite excited, and his strange eyes began to shine like stars and looked more immense than ever.
“They have to please me,” he said. “I’ll make them take me there, and I’ll let you come too.”
Mary wrung her hands together. Everything would be ruined—everything! Dickon would never come back. She would never again feel like a missel thrush with a safe, hidden nest.
“Oh, don’t—don’t—don’t—don’t do that!” she cried out.
He stared as if he thought she had gone crazy!
“Why?” he exclaimed. “You said you wanted to see it.”
“I do,” she answered, a sob almost catching in her throat, “but if you force them to open the door and carry you in that way, it can never be a secret again.”
He leaned still farther forward.
“A secret,” he said. “What do you mean? Tell me.”
Mary’s words almost tumbled over one another.

“You see—you see,” she panted, “suppose no one knew except us—suppose there was a door, hidden somewhere under the ivy—suppose there was—and we could find it; and suppose we could slip through it together and shut it behind us, so that no one knew anyone was inside. Suppose we called it our garden and pretended that—that we were missel thrushes and it was our nest. And suppose we played there almost every day and dug and planted seeds and made it all come alive—”
“Is it dead?” he interrupted her.
“It soon will be if no one takes care of it,” she went on. “The bulbs will live, but the roses—”
He stopped her again, as excited as she was herself.
“What are bulbs?” he put in quickly.
“They’re daffodils and lilies and snowdrops. They’re working in the earth now—pushing up pale green points because spring is coming.”
“Is spring coming?” he said. “What is it like? You can’t see it in a room if you’re ill.”

“Think of the sun shining on the rain and the rain falling through the sunshine, and of everything pushing up and working away under the earth,” said Mary. “If the garden were a secret and we found a way in, we could watch things grow a little bigger each day and count how many roses are still alive. Don’t you see? Oh, don’t you see how much nicer it would be as a secret?”
He dropped back onto his pillow and lay there with a strange look on his face.
“I never had a secret,” he said, “except the one about not living to grow up. They don’t know that I know about it, so it’s a sort of secret. But I like this kind better.”

“If you won’t make them take you to the garden,” Mary pleaded, “then maybe—I feel almost sure I can find out how to get in sometime. And then—if the doctor wants you to go out in your chair, and if you can always do what you want—maybe we could find some boy who would push you, and we could go there alone, and it would always be a secret garden.”
“I would—like—that,” he said very slowly, his eyes growing dreamy. “I would like that. I wouldn’t mind fresh air in a secret garden.”

Mary began to catch her breath and feel safer, because the idea of keeping the secret seemed to please him. She felt almost sure that if she kept talking, and could make him see the garden in his mind the way she had seen it, he would like it so much that he couldn’t stand the thought of everybody tramping in whenever they pleased.
“I’ll tell you what I _think_ it would be like, if we could go into it,” she said. “It has been shut up for so long that perhaps everything has grown into a tangle.”

He lay perfectly still and listened as she went on talking about the roses that _might_ have climbed from tree to tree and hung down, and about the many birds that _might_ have built their nests there because it was so safe. Then she told him about the robin and Ben Weatherstaff. There was so much to tell about the robin, and it was so easy and safe to talk about, that she stopped feeling afraid. The robin pleased him so much that he smiled until he looked almost beautiful. At first Mary had thought he was even plainer than she was, with his big eyes and his heavy locks of hair.
“I didn’t know birds could be like that,” he said. “But if you stay in a room, you never see things. You know so many things! I feel as if you had been inside that garden.”
She didn’t know what to say, so she said nothing. He plainly didn’t expect an answer, and a moment later he surprised her.
“I’m going to let you look at something,” he said. “Do you see that rose-colored silk curtain hanging on the wall over the mantelpiece?”
Mary hadn’t noticed it before, but now she looked up and saw it. It was a curtain of soft silk, hanging over what seemed to be a picture.
“Yes,” she answered.
“There’s a cord hanging from it,” said Colin. “Go and pull it.”

Mary got up, very puzzled, and found the cord. When she pulled it, the silk curtain slid back on its rings and uncovered a picture. It was a picture of a girl with a laughing face. Her bright hair was tied up with a blue ribbon, and her happy, lovely eyes were exactly like Colin’s unhappy ones—agate gray, and looking twice as big as they really were because of the black lashes all around them.
“She’s my mother,” said Colin, in a complaining voice. “I don’t see why she had to die. Sometimes I hate her for doing it.”
“How strange!” said Mary.

“If she had lived, I believe I wouldn’t have been sick all the time,” he grumbled. “I suppose I would have lived, too. And my father wouldn’t have hated to look at me. I suppose I would have had a strong back. Draw the curtain again.”
Mary did as she was told and went back to her footstool.
“She’s much prettier than you are,” she said, “but her eyes are just like yours. They’re the same shape and color, at least. Why did you have the curtain pulled over her?”
He shifted uncomfortably.
“I made them do it,” he said. “Sometimes I don’t like to see her looking at me. She smiles too much when I’m sick and miserable. Besides, she’s mine, and I don’t want everyone to see her.”
There were a few moments of silence, and then Mary spoke.
“What would Mrs. Medlock do if she found out I had been here?” she asked.
“She would obey me,” he answered. “I would tell her I want you to come and talk to me every day. I’m glad you came.”
“So am I,” said Mary. “I’ll come as often as I can, but”—she hesitated—“I’ll have to look every day for the garden door.”
“Yes, you must,” said Colin, “and afterward you can tell me about it.”
He lay thinking for a few minutes, as he had done before, and then he spoke again.
“I think you should be a secret, too,” he said. “I won’t say anything until they find out on their own. I can always send the nurse from the room and tell her I want to be alone. Do you know Martha?”
“Yes, I know her very well,” said Mary. “She waits on me.”
He nodded toward the outer corridor.

“She’s the one who is asleep in the other room. The nurse went away yesterday to spend the night with her sister, and whenever she wants to go out, she always makes Martha look after me. Martha will tell you when to come here.”
Then Mary understood why Martha had looked so troubled when she had asked questions about the crying.
“Martha knew about you all the time?” she said.
“Yes. She often looks after me. The nurse likes to get away from me, and then Martha comes.”
“I’ve been here a long time,” said Mary. “Should I go now? Your eyes look sleepy.”
“I wish I could fall asleep before you leave me,” he said, rather shyly.
“Shut your eyes,” said Mary, drawing her footstool closer, “and I’ll do what my Ayah used to do in India. I’ll pat your hand and stroke it and sing something very softly.”
“I think I might like that,” he said drowsily.

For some reason she felt sorry for him and didn’t want him to lie awake. So she leaned against the bed and began to stroke and pat his hand, and she sang a very quiet little chanting song in Hindustani.

“That’s nice,” he said, even more drowsily. She went on chanting and stroking, but when she looked at him again, his black lashes were lying close against his cheeks, for his eyes were shut and he was fast asleep. So she got up softly, took her candle, and crept away without making a sound.
